questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a personal act of the sovereign.
questions.stem: Tide pool log, 14 March. I watched the assembly's Speaker sign a declaration that closed the winter collection season, and I noted that no vote of the assembly was required. Which description fits that act best?

options.text: A personal act of the sovereign, because it is issued in the sovereign's own name and needs no vote.
A delegated rule, because the assembly had already given the Speaker a general power of this kind.
options.misconception: treats a personal act as an exercise of delegated power

options.text: A committee decision, because the collection committee had recommended the declaration earlier.
options.misconception: assumes a recommendation makes the act a committee decision

options.text: An order of the assembly, because the Speaker signs in the assembly's name at every sitting.
options.misconception: confuses the Speaker's own name with the assembly's name

questions.explanation: A personal act is done in the sovereign's own name and needs no parliamentary vote, unlike an order of the assembly. The reading that it is a delegated rule misses that no general power is exercised.
questions.hint: Done in the sovereign's own name.

questions.learningObjective: Identify an acting head appointed by convention.

stimulus.body: Notice from the Clerk: the Head of the Tidepool Council has resigned, to take effect at the end of the month. options.misconception: reads an automatic convention as an election

The office is left vacant, because the acting appointment requires a vote that has not been held.
options.misconception: assumes a vote is needed for the acting appointment

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the executive is elected indirectly.
questions.stem: Explain how the executive of our assembly is elected indirectly, and what the indirect step is actually for.

answer.exemplar: Our executive is elected in two steps. The first step is the direct one: the whole membership votes for a slate of candidates, and the slate with a majority is returned to the assembly. The second step is the indirect one: the assembly then chooses from that slate to form the executive, taking its members from among the returned candidates and rejecting the rest. The purpose of the indirect step is to allow a broad settlement to be corrected by a smaller body without appealing to the membership again. The first vote produces a set of people the membership broadly accepts; the second asks whether that set can actually work together as a government. The cost of the indirect step is delay, and the risk that the assembly chooses a narrower group than the membership intended.

questions.explanation: The direct vote returns a broad slate and the assembly selects a working executive from it, correcting a broad choice into a workable one. The complaint that the indirect step is undemocratic ignores the first vote.
questions.hint: A slate is returned; the executive is picked from it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: An electorate smaller than the country
questions.learningObjective: Compare the electorate with the affected population.

stimulus.body: Extract from the franchise note: the membership roll of the rockpool society consists of the named holders of a share in the society, being 640 persons. All members of the wider coastal community of 12,000 inhabitants are affected by the assembly's decisions, but only the named holders may vote on them.

questions.stem: According to the note, what is the relationship between the electorate and the population affected by the decisions?

options.text: The electorate is a small group of 640 out of a community of 12,000 affected by the decisions.
The electorate and the affected population are the same, since decisions bind only those who may vote.
options.misconception: assumes decisions bind only those who vote on them

options.text: The electorate is larger, since every adult in the community may apply to join the roll.
options.misconception: assumes the roll is open to the whole community

options.text: The two figures cannot be compared, since the note measures the community in a different unit.
options.misconception: invents a unit mismatch the note does not create

questions.explanation: Six hundred and forty voters decide matters affecting twelve thousand people, so the electorate is a small minority of the affected population. The assumption that decisions bind only voters ignores that they reach everyone.
questions.hint: Compare 640 with 12,000.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the record of dissolutions.
questions.stem: Dissolution record for the rockpool society: in 27 years of assembly history, dissolutions have been held 4 times, and each has been followed within five months by an election in which the party that dissolved the assembly lost seats. What does this pattern show?

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a minority cabinet survives.
questions.stem: Why can a cabinet that lacks a legislative majority continue in office, and what keeps such an arrangement stable?

options.text: Because the constitution allows the sovereign to appoint any cabinet at the head of a minority vote.
options.misconception: attributes the arrangement to the sovereign's appointment power

options.text: Because a cabinet that is tolerated must still win the next budget vote to remain in office.
options.misconception: assumes a tolerated cabinet faces a no-confidence vote at once

options.text: Because the constitution permits it and no alternative majority exists that the assembly would accept.
Because a dissolved assembly leaves the cabinet in place until a new one can be formed.
options.misconception: treats dissolution as the mechanism sustaining a minority cabinet

questions.explanation: A minority cabinet survives where the constitution allows one and no acceptable majority alternative exists, so it rests on other parties' calculations. The claim that a no-confidence vote follows at once misstates how it works.
questions.hint: Nobody else can form a majority.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Set out the opposition's strategic arithmetic.
questions.stem: Using our membership's figures, set out how the opposition should think about its own chances, and what would change the arithmetic.

answer.exemplar: The opposition's arithmetic begins with the seats it holds. Ours has 19 of 40, so it is two seats short of the 21 needed for a bare majority, and short of the 24 that would give it a comfortable working majority. The second step is to ask what the other blocs will do, which is where arithmetic runs out and judgement begins. If the three moderates who defected last year are prepared to support a budget that protects the coastal leases, 19 plus 3 gives the 22 the government needs and the opposition is not the government at all. The third step is the disciplined one: a party that expects to win should not have to reach for a partner with different priorities, because such an alliance costs more in the second budget than it gains in the first. So the honest conclusion is that the opposition cannot win on 19 seats alone and must either persuade a bloc on its own terms or wait for the electoral arithmetic to shift.

questions.explanation: With 19 of 40 seats the opposition is short of a majority and must persuade others or wait, and alliances have costs. Assuming support from a potential ally ignores its price in later budgets.
questions.hint: Count seats, then count partners.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Draw conclusions from an exactly tied division.

stimulus.body: Division list from the assembly's sitting: on the motion to widen the protected reef zone, 21 members voted for, 21 voted against, and no abstentions were recorded. The Speaker, having voted with the majority, did not exercise a casting vote on this occasion.

questions.stem: From the division list, which conclusion can properly be drawn?

options.text: The motion was carried, because the Speaker did not cast a deciding vote of any kind.
options.misconception: infers the result from the absence of a casting vote

options.text: The motion was defeated, because a tied division is not carried without a casting vote.
The motion was carried, because a Speaker who votes with the majority carries it by definition.
options.misconception: assumes the Speaker's vote is always a casting vote

options.text: The division must be repeated, because a tie is always an irregularity requiring a fresh vote.
options.misconception: assumes a tie requires the division to be repeated

questions.explanation: A tied division is not carried unless the Speaker casts a deciding vote, and the list records none, so the motion fell. The assumption that a Speaker's majority vote is a casting vote ignores what casting means.
questions.hint: A tie needs a casting vote to carry.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the acting head convention matters.
questions.stem: Explain why the convention of an acting head matters so much, and what happens if it is not followed properly.

answer.exemplar: The convention of an acting head matters because there must always be someone with the legal authority to act, and a vacancy with nobody qualified to sign, appoint or convene would suspend the ordinary business of the assembly. The convention answers the gap between a resignation taking effect and a successor being chosen, which under our practice takes a full sitting cycle. The rules of the convention are therefore strict. The acting head must hold the office that the convention names, and no one else may assume its duties, however senior they are, because an informal assumption of authority creates two claimants and no way to settle the dispute. If the convention were ignored, the assembly would have to pass a special resolution to appoint someone, which is slow, and the risk is that a person acts without the authority of their office.

questions.explanation: The acting head guarantees lawful authority exists between a resignation and a successor being chosen. Letting the most senior person step in informally risks two claimants and acts that can be challenged.
questions.hint: Someone must be authorised at all times.

options.misconception: treats the election as a direct choice of a leader

options.misconception: denies any effect to the returned slate

options.text: A slate of candidates from which the assembly must then choose the executive.

questions.explanation: The rule makes the general election return a slate of candidates, with the assembly choosing the executive from among them afterwards. The reading that the election produces the executive directly misses the required slate.
questions.hint: The election returns a slate, not a government.

options.misconception: assumes the assembly cannot agree to end its own term

Because the head of the executive is the only person who can be impeached by the assembly.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a minority cabinet governs.
questions.stem: Explain how a minority cabinet can govern at all, and why the arrangement is described as tolerated rather than legitimate.

answer.exemplar: A minority cabinet governs by making the arithmetic work rather than by claiming a mandate. It survives on the arithmetic of the chamber, which means its budgets must be negotiated, its appointments agreed, and its measures shaped to win the support it lacks. Where the constitution permits a minority government, the minority can also govern by spending decisions and by administrative action, which rarely require a legislative majority and which can build a record that later makes a majority possible. The word tolerated is the important one. Tolerance is not a claim that the cabinet has the right to govern; it is an absence of a decision to remove it. The arrangement holds because the parties that could end it calculate that alternatives are worse than the inconvenience of the status quo, and that calculation can change at any moment.

questions.explanation: A minority cabinet governs by negotiation and administrative action while its survival rests on others' calculations, so tolerance is temporary rather than a mandate. Calling it legitimate overstates mere absence of removal.
questions.hint: Tolerance is not a right to govern.

questions.hint: Two seats, and what they cost.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the casting vote works and why it is neutral.
questions.stem: Explain how the casting vote works, and why it is normally given to a presiding officer rather than to the government.

answer.exemplar: A casting vote is the vote a presiding officer exercises when the division is exactly tied. It exists because without it every tied division would end in a dead end, and the assembly would have to devise a fresh procedure each time one arose, which would let the outcome depend on the accident of numbers and on whoever happened to be in the chair. The reason the vote is generally given to a neutral presiding officer rather than to the government is that a casting vote exercised by a partisan would let a government decide every tie in its own favour, which would distort the balance of the chamber at precisely the moments when the balance is closest. The difficulty of the alternatives is that they give the parties a veto over the outcome, since a government which loses a tie might then find the division reversed on a recount.

questions.explanation: Giving the casting vote to a neutral chair stops it distorting the chamber, unlike a government vote. The objection that it overpowers the chair overlooks the vetoes alternatives create.
questions.hint: Only where no majority is apparent.

questions.explanation: The note bars anyone active in the contested election, a neutrality rule rather than a limit on the office. The assumption that the Chair takes over, or the Sovereign acts personally, is absent from it.
questions.hint: Look for the exclusion clause.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the case for the dissolution power.
questions.stem: Set out the case for and against giving the head of the executive the power to dissolve the assembly, and reach a conclusion.

answer.exemplar: The case for the dissolution power is that it gives the head a means of seeking a fresh verdict when the existing assembly has lost its authority, and that the electorate, which owns the assembly's mandate, is the proper body to renew it. Without it, a broken assembly can limp on indefinitely, and every attempt to break it up becomes a negotiation between the parties with the most to lose from the change. The case against is that the temptation is overwhelming: a head about to lose a vote on a budget or a confidence motion may prefer the prospect of a fresh election, even one it expects to lose, to a defeat that would end the government. And the historical record shows how rarely dissolutions repay the gamble, with each in our society followed by losses for those who called one. The conclusion is to keep the power but to require it to be exercised on a stated ground, so that the reason is on the record.

questions.explanation: The dissolution power enables a fresh verdict but its temptation is real and the record shows it rarely pays, so it needs a stated ground. The argument that only the head can seek a mandate ignores the risk of dodging defeat.
questions.hint: Keep it, but require a stated reason.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a personal act from an order of the assembly.
questions.stem: Explain what distinguishes a personal act of the Sovereign from an order of the assembly, and why the distinction matters in practice.

answer.exemplar: A personal act of the Sovereign is an act done in the Sovereign's own name and on the Sovereign's own authority, which the constitution entrusts to that office personally; the appointment of certain officers, the reception of ambassadors and the granting of pardons are examples. An order of the assembly requires the assembly to have resolved, and it depends on the assembly continuing to think it right. The distinction matters in practice because the two can be exercised by different people and on different timetables, and because the register distinguishes them. A minister may make a rule by delegated power between sittings and yet owe the assembly an explanation; the Sovereign may act alone; the assembly may legislate only by its own vote. Where the register does not distinguish an act from an order, a later argument about who authorised a measure becomes impossible to settle.

questions.explanation: A personal act rests on the Sovereign's own authority and needs no vote, while an order depends on an assembly resolution, and the register shows which is which. The assumption that both are interchangeable ignores who is responsible.
questions.hint: Who is responsible: the Sovereign or the assembly?

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the conditions on a lawful casting vote.

stimulus.body: Extract from the Speaker's note: the Speaker's casting vote is exercised only where the division is exactly equal and only where no majority is apparent on the Speaker's own count; it may not be exercised to support a measure the Speaker has spoken against, and the fact of its exercise is entered in the minutes with the reason.

questions.stem: Under the note, which of the following describes a lawful exercise of the casting vote?

options.text: Casting for a measure the Speaker has spoken against, since the duty requires a decision either way.
options.misconception: overreads the duty to decide as removing the neutrality limit

options.text: Casting on an exactly equal division where no majority is apparent, and recording the reason.
Casting to settle a dispute about procedure, since the Speaker's ruling on procedure is final.
options.misconception: confuses a procedural ruling with a casting vote

options.text: Casting to break a tie in a division that stood at 22 votes each before an abstention was recorded.
options.misconception: treats an unequal division after an abstention as a tie

questions.explanation: The note permits a casting vote only on an exactly equal division with no apparent majority, and the reason must be minuted. Treating a ruling as a casting vote confuses two functions, and an abstention means the division was not a tie.
questions.hint: Exactly equal, no apparent majority.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: An electorate smaller than the country
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the case for widening the franchise.
questions.stem: Weigh the arguments for widening the franchise of our society, and give me a conclusion for the log.

answer.exemplar: The case for widening the franchise is a matter of plain justice. Six hundred and forty share holders decide questions of rates, of leases and of the management of the foreshore, and twelve thousand people live with the consequences of those decisions, most of them without any way to influence them. Where the burden of a decision falls on the whole community, the argument for including the whole community is strongest, and a franchise defended by fees as well as shares compounds the exclusion by price as well as by property. The case against is that the members hold the society together: they pay for the equipment, they maintain the buildings, they carry the liability, and a widened franchise might bring in people who wish to enjoy those assets without accepting responsibility for them. The conclusion is that the franchise should be widened, but by admitting the people who live in the coastal community and hold the ordinary leases.

questions.explanation: Widening the franchise is justified because those affected lack influence, while the case against turns on responsibility for shared assets. The temptation to leave the franchise alone ignores that exclusion by price compounds exclusion by property.
questions.hint: Widening must keep responsibility intact.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of indirect election on representation.
questions.stem: Explain what an indirect election of the executive does to the relationship between the membership and the government it produces.

answer.exemplar: An indirect election inserts a second decision between the membership and the government, and that changes the relationship in two directions. In the first place it moderates the mandate: the membership chooses a slate rather than a working team, so it endorses a direction without endorsing a particular combination, and the assembly may then pick a combination that the membership did not specifically endorse. The executive can therefore claim that it has been chosen by the membership without having been chosen by it. In the second place it costs the executive the claim that it speaks directly for the voters, so an executive that owes its position to a slate rather than to the people may be more acceptable to the membership but less legitimate in its own eyes. The intermediary stage is not a formality: it is the place where a broad electoral verdict is turned into a workable government.

questions.explanation: The second stage moderates the mandate and weakens the executive's claim to speak directly for the voters, the real cost of the arrangement. The claim that it is a formality ignores where the judgement is made.
questions.hint: Two decisions, and a weaker mandate.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Advise an opposition short of a majority.
questions.stem: Explain what the opposition should do when it is short of a majority but holds more seats than any other bloc in the assembly.

answer.exemplar: The opposition's arithmetic looks different from the government's in one important way: the arithmetic of the government is about whether it can survive, and the arithmetic of the opposition is about whether it can win. Being the largest bloc does not give the opposition the numbers to form a government, and it should not pretend otherwise. The temptation is to seek any partner who will combine, but a government assembled from a reluctant partner at the moment of crisis is a government that will not survive the next crisis, and the parties that combine today will calculate against each other tomorrow. The disciplined course is therefore to work on the seats that can change: to make the case that a change of government is in the interest of the electorate, to hold the government to the issues where it is weakest, and to win over the moderate bloc on terms that do not require abandoning the opposition's own principles.

questions.explanation: The largest bloc still lacks the numbers to govern, and a coalition with a reluctant partner is unstable, so the discipline is to persuade the moderates on terms. The preference for any available ally ignores how such alliances decay.
questions.hint: Largest is not the same as enough.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: An electorate smaller than the country
questions.learningObjective: Explain the interaction of franchise and dissolution.
questions.stem: Explain how a narrow franchise interacts with the dissolution power, and what that interaction means for accountability.

answer.exemplar: A narrow franchise and a dissolution power reinforce each other, and the direction of the effect is not obvious. The connection is the electorate: dissolution sends the decision back to the voters, and if the voters are a small proper body of the affected community, then dissolution returns the decision to a narrow circle while the consequences fall on everyone. A government that is tolerated by a narrow electorate may be more secure than it would be with a broad one, because a small group of holders has interests that are easier to satisfy, and because the threat of an election is less frightening when the electorate is small. So a narrow franchise does not simply weaken legitimacy at the moment of dissolution; it makes the sanction for bad government weak as well, since a government that loses the confidence of a few hundred people has little to fear. Widening the franchise and limiting the dissolution power are two parts of the same project.

questions.explanation: A narrow franchise weakens the electoral sanction for bad government, so dissolution returns the decision to a small body while the costs fall on everyone. The claim that the franchise only matters at a general election ignores its role at a dissolution.
questions.hint: Dissolution returns the decision to the roll.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe the use of the casting vote.
questions.stem: Describe how the casting vote is used in our assembly, and what happens when it is not needed.

answer.exemplar: The casting vote is used only in the one situation it exists for: a division in which the numbers on each side are exactly equal. The Speaker then casts a deciding vote, and the fact that it was exercised, and the reason for it, are entered in the minutes. The Speaker is bound to observe the neutrality rule, so that the vote is not used to support a measure the Speaker has spoken against, and in practice the long-established convention is to vote to retain the status quo rather than to decide a question of principle. Where no casting vote is needed, the matter is simply decided: if there is a majority either way, the division settles it, and if the Speaker's own vote is not part of the division and no majority is apparent, the question can be put again, and it is only the true deadlock that calls for the casting vote to be used.

questions.explanation: The casting vote is used only on an exact tie, subject to neutrality and recorded with its reason. The belief that it decides close divisions confuses a casting vote with an ordinary majority, however narrow.
questions.hint: Only on an exact tie.

questions.topic: An electorate smaller than the country
questions.learningObjective: Explain the stability a narrow franchise can produce.
questions.stem: Why can a narrow franchise make the assembly's decisions more stable, and what is the cost of that stability?

options.text: Because a small body of voters can be persuaded to support a consistent course, at the cost of excluding those most affected.
Because a small electorate makes decisions quicker, since fewer members need to be consulted.
options.misconception: confuses franchise size with the speed of procedure

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Combine dissolution and franchise in one conclusion.
questions.stem: Combine what the dissolution power and the narrow franchise do to political accountability in our society, and draw a conclusion about reform.

answer.exemplar: Taken together, the dissolution power and the narrow franchise determine who is actually answerable for the decisions of the assembly. The dissolution power is the strongest sanction the constitution provides, because it takes the decision away from the people who took it and puts it back to the voters, and no institution can be entirely comfortable with that prospect. The narrow franchise then determines how much the sanction is worth. Our voters are the 640 named holders on the roll, and the community of twelve thousand lives with the results of decisions made by that smaller body. The consequence is that the threat of dissolution, which is severe in form, is mild in substance, because a government that loses the confidence of a small electorate may face few consequences at all. Widening the franchise and limiting the dissolution power are two parts of the same project: each gives the decision back to the people affected by it.

questions.explanation: Dissolution is the strongest sanction, but the narrow franchise makes it mild in substance, so both need reform. The assumption that a strong formal sanction suffices ignores who actually votes in it.
questions.hint: Reform the electorate and the sanction together.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the significance of tolerated rather than legitimate.

options.text: It means the government must hold a fresh election within a year of taking office.
options.misconception: invents an election requirement for minority governments

options.text: It means the government continues on the absence of a decision to remove it, not on any claim of a right to rule.
It means the Sovereign may dismiss the government at any time without giving a cause.
options.misconception: invents a power of dismissal the constitution does not grant

questions.explanation: Tolerance rests on the absence of a decision to remove the government rather than on a claim to rule, which is why it is fragile. The opposition veto, election deadline and power of dismissal are not in the constitution.
questions.hint: Not being removed is not being entitled.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate eliminations needed to select an executive.
questions.stem: Indirect election arithmetic: the general election returns a slate of 24 candidates for 12 executive seats. If the assembly's first ballot produced no majority, how many further candidates must be eliminated before a clear choice of 12 can be made?
questions.explanation: Twelve candidates must be eliminated, since a slate of 24 for 12 seats is twice the size required. The answer of 24 counts the slate rather than the eliminations, and the lack of a first majority does not change the arithmetic.
questions.hint: The slate is twice the number of seats.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Infer the opposition's position from a district map.

stimulus.body: Extract from the district note: the assembly's 40 seats are divided into 5 districts of 8 seats each, and each district returns its members by a first-past-the-post contest among all the candidates in that district. In the last election the governing bloc took 3 districts, the opposition 1, and one district was split 4 to 4 between them.

questions.stem: The note describes a district map. What can be inferred about the opposition's position?

options.text: The opposition is short of control and cannot be sure of the split district, since it is tied there 4 to 4.
The opposition can win the assembly with two more districts, since it holds one district already.
options.misconception: ignores the seat count within a district

options.text: The opposition is the largest bloc, since it holds one district and half of another.
options.misconception: counts a tied district as though it were won outright

options.text: The electoral system has no effect, since every seat is decided on a first-past-the-post basis.
options.misconception: denies that the district system shapes the result

questions.explanation: With one district won and one tied, the opposition holds neither the numbers nor a clear position in the split district, so control is out of reach. The claim that it can win with two districts ignores that a district delivers eight seats.
questions.hint: A district delivers eight seats.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh an unapproved personal act power.
questions.stem: Set out the arguments for and against granting the Sovereign a personal act power that no assembly has approved, and give a conclusion.

answer.exemplar: The case for a personal act power is that some decisions cannot wait for an assembly, and that the constitution needs a point of authority which is not vulnerable to the disagreements of the moment. A sovereign who can act alone between sittings can respond to an emergency, appoint the officers the machinery requires and receive the foreign missions whose arrival cannot be postponed, and none of these needs to be debated to be legitimate. The case against is that any power not made by the assembly is a power not made by the people who are subject to it, and that the older habits of personal government are exactly what a written constitution is meant to displace. The conclusion is that the power should be kept but defined narrowly, listed specifically in the constitution rather than inferred from custom, and reported to the assembly at its next sitting.

questions.explanation: An unapproved personal act power gives continuity where decisions cannot wait, but it must be narrowly listed rather than inferred from custom. Calling such acts ceremonial evades the question of subject matter.
questions.hint: List the powers, do not infer them.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a ground for dissolution in a provision.

stimulus.body: Extract from the constitutional provision: the head of the executive may, if the assembly has twice rejected the supply, or if the assembly has been unable to provide for the service of the year, dissolve the assembly by a proclamation, and thereupon the members shall be returned to their constituencies.

questions.stem: Under the provision above, which of the following is a stated ground for dissolution?

options.text: The head of the executive wishes a fresh verdict from the electorate on its own record.
options.misconception: reads a general wish for a fresh verdict as a stated ground

options.text: The head of the executive has lost a vote of confidence in the assembly by a bare majority.
options.misconception: treats a confidence defeat as a dissolution ground

options.text: The assembly has twice rejected the supply, or has been unable to provide for the service of the year.
The opposition has asked the assembly to consider whether the executive should continue.
options.misconception: mistakes an opposition request for a constitutional ground

questions.explanation: The provision names two grounds, the repeated rejection of supply and the failure to provide for the year. The options, a wish for a fresh verdict, a confidence defeat and an opposition request, are not grounds the text states.
questions.hint: The provision names two grounds.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a record of tolerated governments.
questions.stem: Minority government record: over 14 years of tolerated administrations, the average government bloc held 47 per cent of seats, 11 governments survived a full term, and 3 were replaced after the opposition tabled a confidence motion. What does this show?

options.text: Tolerated governments are usually short-lived, since only 11 of 14 lasted a full term.
options.misconception: counts the full terms as if they were the whole record

options.text: Tolerated governments command a clear majority of the assembly, since 47 per cent is close to half.
options.misconception: treats a near-half bloc as a majority

options.text: Confidence motions are a routine tool, since 3 of 14 governments fell to them.
options.misconception: reads three falls in fourteen as routine use

options.text: Tolerated governments are the normal pattern here, since most survived a full term without a confidence vote.

questions.explanation: Eleven of fourteen governments survived a full term and 3 fell to confidence motions, so tolerance is the normal pattern rather than a crisis. The claim that such governments are short-lived miscounts the record, and 47 per cent is a minority.
questions.hint: Compare the two counts directly.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the case for a presiding casting vote.
questions.stem: Assess the case for and against giving the presiding officer a casting vote, and reach a conclusion for the log.

answer.exemplar: The case for the casting vote is that without it the assembly must solve a deadlock by a fresh and improvised procedure each time one arises, and improvised procedures are decided by whoever is most insistent on a particular one. That is how the assembly's outcomes come to depend on the accident of numbers rather than on the merits, and how a single defection is converted into a victory for whichever side first proposes the convenient formula. The case against is that a casting vote places a decision of real weight in the hands of one person, and that the presiding officer's neutrality is a matter of convention rather than of law, which is a fragile guarantee for so consequential a power. The conclusion is to keep the casting vote and to surround it with conditions: the division must be exactly equal, the Speaker must not have spoken against the measure, the reason must be minuted, and the convention of voting to retain the status quo should be stated in the rules.

questions.explanation: The casting vote avoids improvised deadlock procedures, but it needs strict conditions around neutrality and reasons. The case for abolishing it ignores the deadlocks it would leave unresolved.
questions.hint: Keep it, but ring it with conditions.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Select the arrangement that secures lawful continuity.
questions.stem: Which arrangement best secures the lawful continuity of the office when the head's term ends unexpectedly?

options.text: An election of the acting head at the first sitting held after the vacancy arises.
options.misconception: makes the acting head depend on the speed of the next sitting

options.text: A standing convention naming the person who holds the duties until the assembly chooses a successor.
An instruction from the Sovereign to the Senior Assessor to take the duties in hand.
options.misconception: assumes the Sovereign may direct the acting head

options.text: A provision that no one holds the duties until the assembly has chosen a successor.
options.misconception: asserts a deliberate gap in lawful authority

questions.explanation: A standing convention fills the gap at once and without argument, which is what lawful continuity requires. The alternatives either depend on the speed of the next sitting or leave the office unoccupied, defeating the purpose.
questions.hint: The gap must be filled at once.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: An electorate smaller than the country
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of the community on the roll.
questions.stem: Franchise arithmetic: the society has 640 members on the roll out of a coastal community of 12,000 people, and 480 members voted at the last general election. What percentage of the community is represented on the roll?
questions.explanation: Six hundred and forty of twelve thousand is 5.33 per cent, since 640 divided by 12,000 gives 0.05333. The figures of 40 and 75 relate to turn-out among the roll, not to the share of the community that may vote.
questions.hint: Divide the roll by the community, then convert.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Account for the outcome of an indirect election.

stimulus.body: Extract from the election report: the general election returned a slate of 24 candidates for the 12 seats of the executive; on the first ballot no candidate had a majority, and on the second ballot, after the assembly struck out six names, eleven candidates received the same number of votes and the twelfth was selected by the assembly's choice.

questions.stem: Reading the report, which account of the outcome is correct?

options.text: The executive was the slate the electorate returned, since the assembly only removed names it disliked.
options.misconception: misreads the assembly's selection as the electorate's list

options.text: The executive was elected directly by the membership, since the slate was chosen by them.
options.misconception: confuses returning a slate with electing an executive

options.text: The election produced no executive, because no candidate ever obtained a majority of the membership.
options.misconception: assumes a majority of the membership is required

options.text: The executive was chosen by the assembly from the returned slate, which is an indirect election.

questions.explanation: The report shows the membership returning a slate and the assembly selecting the executive from it, which is an indirect election. The tempting accounts mistake the slate for the executive, or the assembly's choice for a direct election.
questions.hint: Two elections, in sequence.
